title: How To Avoid Losing Control The Final Days Of The School Year f-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin offers a targeted strategy for the notoriously difficult final stretch of the school year, when routines get sloppy and students become distracted by approaching summer. Rather than clamping down harder, he recommends adjusting three specific areas: slowing down transitions with more explicit modeling and a deliberately unhurried demeanor that students will begin to mirror; speeding up routines to combat end-of-year boredom by having students perform them faster or under tighter timers; and pushing academics harder rather than easing off, giving students a head start on next year's material to maintain challenge and engagement. He argues the end of the year should end as a surprise rather than a slow countdown to the finish line. The piece closes by connecting these small structural adjustments to sustained motivation, better behavior, and a stronger finish to the school year.
points: Rather than clamping down harder during the chaotic final stretch of the year, teachers should adjust three specific structural areas: transitions, routines, and academics.
Transitions should be slowed down with more explicit modeling and a deliberately relaxed demeanor, which students tend to mirror over time.
Routines should be sped up — performed faster or with tighter timers — to counter late-year boredom and complacency with familiar procedures.
Academic rigor should increase, not decrease, near year's end, giving students a head start on next-year material to maintain challenge and engagement.
The goal is for the end of the school year to arrive as a surprise rather than feel like a slow, clock-watching trudge to the finish line.
quotes: As the school year draws to a close, voices tend to grow louder. Routines get sloppier. Students become distracted, excitable, and primed for misbehavior.
It’s a happy time, no doubt, but a dangerous one for teachers. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to lose control.
The key here is to slow down. Take more time than usual explaining/modeling what you expect before moving on.
The solution (oddly, given that we want to slow down transitions) is to speed up routines. Model how to perform them double or even triple-time.
Rather than easing up as the year winds down, it’s best to keep pushing. Ask more of your students, not less.
The end of the school year should come as a surprise, not a slow, clock-watching trudge to the finish line.
